source_text: Dei spiritus et dei sermo et dei ratio, sermo rationis et ratio sermonis et spiritus utriusque, Iesus Christus dominus noster nouis discipulis noui testamenti nouam orationis formam determinauit. oportebat enim in hac quoque specie nouum uinum nouis utribus recondi et nouam plagulam nouo adsui uestimento. ceterum quicquid retro fuerat, aut demutatum est, ut circumcisio, aut suppletum, ut reliqua lex, aut impletum, ut prophetia, aut perfectum, ut fides ipsa. omnia de carnalibus in spiritalia renouauit noua dei gratia superducto euangelio, expunctore totius retro uetustatis, in quo et dei spiritus et dei sermo et dei ratio approbatus est dominus noster Iesus Christus, spiritus quo ualuit, sermo quo docuit, ratio qua uenit. sic igitur oratio a Christo constituta ex tribus constituta est: ex sermone, quo enuntiatur, ex spiritu, quo tantum potest, ex ratione, qua docetur. docuerat et Iohannes discipulos suos adorare; sed omnia Iohannis Christo praestruebantur, donec ipso aucto, sicut idem Iohannes praenuntiabat illum augeri oportere, se uero deminui, totum praeministri opus cum ipso spiritu transiret ad dominum. ideo nec extat, in quae uerba docuerit Iohannes adorare, quod terrena caelestibus cesserint. qui de terra est, inquit, terrena fatur, et qui de caelis adest, quae uidit, ea loquitur. et quid non caeleste quod domini Christi est, ut haec quoque orandi disciplina? consideremus itaque, benedicti, caelestem eius sophiam, inprimis de praecepto secrete adorandi, quo et fidem hominis exigebat, ut dei omnipotentis et conspectum et auditum sub tectis et in abditum etiam adesse confideret, et modestiam fidei desiderabat, ut, quem ubique audire et uidere fideret, ei soli religionem suam offerret. sequens sophia III sequenti praecepto perinde pertineat ad fidem et modestiam fidei, si non agmine uerborum adeundum putemus ad dominum, quem ultro suis prospicere certi sumus. et tamen breuitas ista, quod ad tertium sophiae gradum faciat, magnae ac beatae interpretationis substantia fulta est quantumque substringitur uerbis, tantum diffunditur sensibus. \' neque enim propria tantum orationis officia complexa est, uenerationem dei aut hominis petitionem, sed omnem paene sermonem domini, omnem commemorationem disciplinae, ut reuera in oratione breuiarium totius euangelii comprehendatur.
thought_title: The Lord's Prayer as the new form of prayer and summary of the gospel
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by presenting the Lord's Prayer as the new form of prayer Christ gave to his new disciples, replacing and fulfilling all that came before.
pass_a_gloss: The Spirit of God and the word of God and the reason of God, the word of reason and the reason of the word and the Spirit of both, Jesus Christ our Lord, determined a new form of prayer for the new disciples of the new testament. For it was fitting that in this kind also new wine be stored in new wineskins and a new patch be sewn onto a new garment. But whatever had been before was either changed, as circumcision, or completed, as the rest of the law, or fulfilled, as prophecy, or perfected, as faith itself. The new grace of God renewed all things from carnal things into spiritual things, the gospel having been brought in, the canceller of all oldness that was before, in which gospel both the Spirit of God and the word of God and the reason of God was approved as our Lord Jesus Christ, the Spirit by which he was powerful, the word by which he taught, the reason by which he came. Thus therefore the prayer established by Christ was established from three things: from the word, by which it is uttered, from the Spirit, by which alone it is powerful, from the reason, by which it is taught. John also had taught his disciples to pray; but all things of John were being built up beforehand for Christ, until, he himself having increased, just as the same John was foretelling that he ought to increase, but that he himself should decrease, the whole work of the forerunner with the Spirit himself should pass over to the Lord. Therefore it does not even appear in what words John taught to pray, because earthly things yielded to heavenly things. He who is from the earth, he says, speaks earthly things, and he who is present from the heavens speaks those things which he has seen. And what is not heavenly that is of the Lord Christ, as also this teaching of praying? Let us consider therefore, blessed ones, his heavenly wisdom, first of all concerning the precept of praying secretly, by which he both demanded the faith of a person, so that he would trust that the sight and hearing of almighty God is present even under roofs and even in a hidden place, and he desired the modesty of faith, so that, the one whom he trusted to hear and see everywhere, to him alone he should offer his worship. The following wisdom, in the following precept, likewise pertains to faith and the modesty of faith, if we should not think that we must approach the Lord with a crowd of words, whom we are certain looks after his own of his own accord. And yet this brevity, because it makes for the third step of wisdom, is supported by the substance of a great and blessed interpretation, and as much as it is drawn together in words, so much it is spread out in meanings. For it has embraced not only the proper duties of prayer, the veneration of God or the petition of a person, but almost every word of the Lord, every remembrance of the teaching, so that truly in the prayer a summary of the whole gospel is comprehended.

choices.why: Keeps 'form' as the literal shape or pattern Christ fixed, matching the treatise's concern with the Lord's Prayer as the model.

choices.english: the canceller of all oldness that was before
choices.why: Expunctor is a striking metaphor of blotting out or erasing; 'canceller' preserves the literal force of wiping away the old order.
rejected: the eraser of all past antiquity
the one who blotted out all former oldness

choices.why: Modestia here means restraint and humility in approaching God; 'modesty' keeps the literal term and its ethical force.

choices.english: a summary of the whole gospel
choices.why: Breuiarium is a compendium or abridgement; 'summary' conveys the literal sense of the whole gospel compressed into the prayer.
rejected: an abridgement of the entire gospel
a digest of the whole gospel

pass_b_english: The Spirit of God, the Word of God, and the Reason of God—the Word of Reason, the Reason of the Word, and the Spirit of both—Jesus Christ our Lord, determined a new form of prayer for the new disciples of the new covenant. For in this matter too it was fitting that new wine be stored in new wineskins and a new patch be sewn onto a new garment (Matthew 9:17). Whatever had existed before was either changed, like circumcision, or completed, like the rest of the law, or fulfilled, like prophecy, or perfected, like faith itself. The new grace of God renewed all things from carnal to spiritual by introducing the gospel, the canceller of all oldness that was before. In this gospel our Lord Jesus Christ was approved as the Spirit of God, the Word of God, and the Reason of God: the Spirit by which he had power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which he came.

So then, the prayer established by Christ is established from three things: from the word by which it is spoken, from the Spirit by which alone it has power, and from the reason by which it is taught. John had also taught his disciples to pray, but all the things of John were being built up beforehand for Christ, until Christ was increased—John himself foretold that Christ must increase and John must decrease (John 3:30)—and the whole work of the forerunner passed over with his spirit to the Lord. Therefore it is not recorded in what words John taught people to pray, because earthly things yielded to heavenly things. John says, "He who is from the earth speaks earthly things, and he who comes from heaven speaks what he has seen" (John 3:31). And what belonging to the Lord Christ is not heavenly, as this teaching on prayer also is?

Let us consider, then, blessed ones, his heavenly wisdom. First, concerning the command to pray in secret, by which he both demanded the faith of a person—so that one would trust that the sight and hearing of almighty God are present even under roofs and in a hidden place—and desired the modesty of faith, so that the one whom a person trusts to hear and see everywhere would receive that person's worship for himself alone. The wisdom that follows in the next command likewise pertains to faith and the modesty of faith, if we do not think we must approach the Lord with a flood of words, since we are certain that he looks upon us of his own accord. And yet this brevity, which makes for the third step of wisdom, is supported by the substance of a great and blessed interpretation, and as much as it is compressed in words, so much it is expanded in meanings. For it has not only embraced the proper duties of prayer—the worship of God or the petition of a person—but nearly every word of the Lord and every remembrance of his teaching, so that truly in this prayer a summary of the whole gospel is contained.

problems.quote: the Spirit by which he had power
problems.why: Latin says the Spirit gives power to the prayer, not to Christ; English shifts agency to Christ.
problems.fix: the Spirit by which the prayer alone has power
problems.ruling: Context is the prayer: 'quo tantum potest' means the Spirit by which the prayer has power, not Christ.

problems.quote: the Reason by which he came
problems.why: Latin links Reason to teaching (the prayer is taught), English links it to Christ’s coming.
problems.fix: the Reason by which the prayer is taught
problems.ruling: 'ratio qua docetur' = the reason by which the prayer is taught, not 'the Reason by which he came'.

edits.old: the Spirit by which he had power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which he came.
edits.new: the Spirit by which the prayer alone has power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which the prayer is taught.

fixed: Agency: source 'ex spiritu, quo tantum potest' refers to the prayer's power, not Christ's; corrected.
Modality: source 'ratio qua docetur' refers to the prayer being taught, not Christ's coming; corrected.

problems.quote: the Spirit by which the prayer alone has power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which the prayer is taught
problems.source_quote: spiritus quo ualuit, sermo quo docuit, ratio qua uenit
problems.why: All three relatives refer to Christ: Spirit by which he had power, Word by which he taught, Reason by which he came.
problems.fix: the Spirit by which he had power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which he came
problems.ruling: Latin clauses refer to Christ (spiritus quo ualuit, sermo quo docuit, ratio qua uenit); English misassigns to prayer

problems.why: ipso aucto is ablative absolute: 'until he [Christ] was increased.' 'he himself' wrongly implies John was increased.
problems.ruling: Ablative absolute ‘donec ipso aucto’ refers to Christ’s increase; English ‘he himself’ suggests John

problems.quote: since we are certain that he looks after his own of his own accord
problems.source_quote: quem ultro suis prospicere certi sumus
problems.why: English garbles Latin meaning; agency and object are lost, making the sentence unintelligible.
problems.fix: since we are certain that he looks upon us of his own accord
problems.ruling: ultro means 'voluntarily'; suis prospicere means 'to provide for his own'. English 'looks after his own of his own accord' accurately renders this, so claim is false.

edits.old: the Spirit by which the prayer alone has power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which the prayer is taught
edits.new: the Spirit by which he had power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which he came

edits.old: since we are certain that he looks after his own of his own accord
edits.new: since we are certain that he looks upon us of his own accord

fixed: Corrected the three relatives to refer to Christ: 'spiritus quo ualuit, sermo quo docuit, ratio qua uenit' = Spirit by which he had power, Word by which he taught, Reason by which he came.
Corrected 'ipso aucto' as ablative absolute referring to Christ: 'until he [Christ] was increased.'
Corrected 'quem ultro suis prospicere certi sumus' to 'since we are certain that he looks upon us of his own accord.'

problems.why: 'ut' introduces a result clause ('so that even this teaching of prayer is not heavenly?'); 'including' misreads the construction.
problems.fix: so that even this teaching of prayer is not heavenly?
problems.ruling: "ut haec quoque orandi disciplina" means "so that even this discipline of prayer", not "including this teaching of prayer".

edits.old: And what is not heavenly that belongs to the Lord Christ, including this teaching of prayer?
edits.new: And what is not heavenly that belongs to the Lord Christ, so that even this teaching of prayer is not heavenly?

fixed: Changed 'including this teaching of prayer' to 'so that even this teaching of prayer is not heavenly?' because the source 'ut haec quoque orandi disciplina' is a result clause, not an appositive; 'including' misread the construction.

problems.quote: he [Christ] was increased—as John himself foretold, that he must increase and he himself must decrease
problems.why: Bracketed gloss is helpful but the pronoun chain (he/himself/he) is still confusing.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'Christ was increased—John himself foretold that Christ must increase and John must decrease.'

edits.old: until he [Christ] was increased—as John himself foretold, that he must increase and he himself must decrease (John 3:30)—and the whole work of the forerunner passed over with his spirit to the Lord.
edits.new: until Christ was increased—John himself foretold that Christ must increase and John must decrease (John 3:30)—and the whole work of the forerunner passed over with his spirit to the Lord.

fixed: Clarified the pronoun chain in the John the Baptist passage: source 'donec ipso aucto, sicut idem Iohannes praenuntiabat illum augeri oportere, se uero deminui' refers to Christ increasing and John decreasing; the English now names both explicitly.

fixed.quote: what is not heavenly that belongs to the Lord Christ, so that even this teaching of prayer is not heavenly?
fixed.fix: what belonging to the Lord Christ is not heavenly, as this teaching on prayer also is?
fixed.note: The English wrongly implies that the teaching on prayer is not heavenly. The Latin says it is heavenly like everything else of Christ's.

dismissed.quote: would receive that person's worship for himself alone
dismissed.why: Reverses who offers worship; Latin says the worshiper offers his worship to God alone.
dismissed.note: Recasting the sentence as 'God receives the worship' keeps the meaning that the worshiper offers it to him alone; the wording is clunky but not a reversal.

polish.changed: Clarified that John the Baptist is the speaker of the quotation about earthly and heavenly speech, and broke the dense opening into clearer paragraphs.

notes.why: Reader cannot tell if 'he' is Christ, John, or the evangelist.
notes.fix: Specify: 'John says of the earthly man'.
